records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. RHS's dedicated Ficus pumila page gives 'creeping fig' as the rendered subtitle beneath its H1, and NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox publishes a dedicated page titled 'Creeping Fig' (listing 'Climbing Fig' as its sole Other Common Name). Conversely, Clemson HGIC's dedicated factsheet is titled 'Climbing Fig' and calls creeping fig 'its other common name,' and NC State also publishes a second dedicated page for the same species titled 'Climbing Fig' (listing 'Creeping Fig' as its Other Common Name). Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder's structured Common Name field value is 'climbing fig,' though the same page's prose calls the species 'commonly called creeping fig.' This record follows the RHS subtitle and NC State's creeping-fig-titled page and uses 'Creeping Fig.'
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's structured Problems field names this species a 'Problem for Cats', a 'Problem for Dogs' and a 'Problem for Horses'; cats and dogs are named specifically, and the horse tag, which is outside this schema's cat/dog scope, does not diminish the other two. NC State publishes no Poison block for this species, so there is no severity rating, symptom list, toxic principle or poison-part list to reproduce. The hazards the sources do carry are handling hazards, all from the plant's latex: NC State's Stem Description states 'Stems have a milky sap.'; RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Skin allergen.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and carries no 'Pets:' line for this taxon, so that warning is human-scoped; and Clemson HGIC states 'Gloves offer protection from the latex in climbing fig, which may cause dermatitis.' On edibility, NC State's Edibility field states the fruit is 'Not usually grown for edible fruit, but properly prepared it is popular in Asian countries,' but three other passages disagree: its own Fruit Description says 'They are insipid and not worth eating.', its Description paragraph says 'Inedible figs appear after the spring flowers on plants grown outdoors.', and Clemson HGIC states 'Fertilized female flowers produce pale green, pearlike inedible fruit.' Only the structured Edibility field supports a prepared-fruit use.

No admissible source gives a clear category.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are all left null: no admissible source frames watering with a day-interval, a soil-check depth, or a growing/dormant day count for this species.

humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max are all left null: no admissible source gives a numeric humidity, footcandle, or direct-sun-hours figure specific to this species; NC State's Light Requirement categories carry only the site-wide legend's generic hour ranges, which are excluded from direct_sun_hours_max by rule. humidity_need is split out of this entry and set to high, from NC State's own species prose 'It does best in high humidity.'

outdoor_sun_exposure drops full_shade. Clemson HGIC's 'Climbing fig thrives in full sun or shade.' was read as supporting part_shade only: the page says shade, not full shade, and the same paragraph attaches a species-specific caveat ('Vines growing in open, west- or south-facing locations and exposed to cold, wind, and direct sun, may be affected by winter leaf scorch.'). Three structured sun fields exclude a full-shade value -- NC State's Light field, whose deepest value is Partial Shade; RHS's Position field, whose only value is Full sun; and MoBot's Sun field, whose only value is Part shade.

is_edible is set true for the prepared-fruit use per NC State's Edibility field, which is the only passage supporting it; three other passages disagree -- NC State's Fruit Description ('They are insipid and not worth eating.'), NC State's Description paragraph ('Inedible figs appear after the spring flowers on plants grown outdoors.'), and Clemson HGIC ('Fertilized female flowers produce pale green, pearlike inedible fruit.'). The contradiction is disclosed in toxicity_detail.

common_name/name_note: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox publishes two duplicate pages for this exact species, one titled 'Creeping Fig' and one titled 'Climbing Fig,' each listing the other name as its single 'Other Common Name.' Clemson HGIC's dedicated factsheet is titled 'Climbing Fig' and calls creeping fig 'its other common name.' Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Common Name field value is 'climbing fig,' though the same page's prose calls the species 'commonly called creeping fig.' This record follows RHS's subtitle and NC State's creeping-fig-titled page. No collision with an already-landed common_name.

mature_height_in_min/max and mature_spread_in_min/max are all left null under the pipeline's climber rule. NC State's Plant Type field for this species reads Houseplant and Vine, its Habit/Form reads Climbing, and its Description says the plant 'will climb 8 to 15 feet high and spread 3 to 6 feet wide' -- a climber takes no mature size in this catalog, whatever figures a page publishes, because a published height for a climber is the distance it travels along its support rather than the plant's own stature. The figures are recorded here and deliberately not used: NC State's Dimensions block renders 'Height: 8 ft. 0 in. - 15 ft. 0 in.' and 'Width: 3 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in.', and RHS's UK Size block gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres.

Cultivation caution (no dedicated schema field): Clemson HGIC warns that the vine's adhesive attachments damage structures on removal -- 'When the vines are removed, these attachments often remain, which mars the structure's appearance. Some surfaces, particularly wood and stucco, may be damaged when the stems are detached.' NC State separately notes the vine 'can cement itself to porous surfaces,' describing the adhesion rather than the damage. This is a structural/wall-damage caution, kept separate from the milky-latex skin-handling warning and from the cat/dog toxicity tags.

Juvenile vs. mature foliage (no dedicated schema field): NC State, Clemson HGIC, and Missouri Botanical Garden all note the small, thin, heart-shaped juvenile leaves seen on climbing/indoor stems differ sharply from the larger, thicker, leathery, fruit-bearing mature foliage described on some pages — the size/light/water fields above reflect the common juvenile/climbing/houseplant form, not the mature fruiting form.

The citation was dropped with the value.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads for this exact species. NC State's Description names the plant "commonly known as the asparagus fern, lace fern, or plumosa fern" (asparagus fern listed first), and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives a single Common Name field reading "asparagus fern." RHS's dedicated page instead renders its subtitle as "fern asparagus," with "asparagus fern" relegated to its secondary Other common names list. "Asparagus Fern" is used here as common_name because it is led by two of the three dedicated single-species pages (NC State and MoBot) against RHS's one.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped, per the page's own heading) rates Poison Severity: Medium, with Poison Symptoms: 'If the berries are ingested, it can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea in humans and pets. Skin irritation can occur from contact with the plant's sap.', Poison Toxic Principle: Sapogenins, Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes, and a Poison Part list complete at two values, Fruits and Sap/Juice. Separately, NC State's structured Problems field carries all six of its values -- Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Weedy -- naming cats and dogs specifically; that tag block is a different structure from the human-scoped Poison block. Two physical hazards are stated together in NC State's Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems section: 'The spines that form along the length of the stem are sharp, and the sap from the plant may cause skin irritation.', followed by the handling warning 'Wear gloves when handling this plant, and keep it out of the reach of children and pets.' Missouri Botanical Garden corroborates the spines in Noteworthy Characteristics: 'Mature stems become woody over time and develop sharp spines.' RHS's Potentially harmful field adds 'Skin allergen; fruits harmful if eaten.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling', which is unscoped by animal and does not on its own establish cat/dog scope. This taxon is not Asparagus officinalis, the edible garden vegetable: NC State's Edibility field for Asparagus setaceus reads 'The berries are poisonous.'
records.cool_rest_note: MoBot's Culture notes: "Does not require winter dormancy, but appreciates a resting period with reduced watering over the winter months."

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_sun: MoBot's Culture prose says the plant is grown 'in full sun to part shade,' but MoBot's own structured Sun field ('Sun: Part shade'), NC State's Light tags, and RHS's Position field ('Partial shade') all agree only on part shade, so full_sun was left out.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: NC State gives only a seasonal cadence ('regular watering in spring to autumn and sparingly in winter') and MoBot gives a structured 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale, not keep_moist) plus a similar seasonal cadence; neither source frames watering as a dry-down target, a check depth, or a numeric day interval.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: none of the admissible sources (NC State, RHS, MoBot) give fertilizing guidance for this species.

attracts_pollinators left null: NC State's Wildlife Value field says only 'Birds eat the berries and disperse the seeds,' which is seed dispersal, not pollination; no admissible source mentions bees, butterflies, or other pollinators for this species.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in use NC State's structured Dimensions block (houseplant scale, 2-3 ft each way) as the anchor, per the rule preferring a dedicated page's own structured dimensions. NC State's unstructured prose ('up to 10 to 20 feet tall' in its native habitat) and MoBot's structured Height (10.00-20.00 feet) describe the stem length of the plant scrambling/climbing on a support in the wild, not its own free-standing size, so those figures were excluded.

This taxon, Asparagus setaceus, is not Asparagus officinalis (the edible garden vegetable); no edibility statement was carried over from that species, and is_edible is set to false only on NC State's own statement for A. setaceus that 'The berries are poisonous.'

toxic_to_pets is scoped to cats and dogs specifically, per NC State's Landscape Problems tags ('Problem for Cats', 'Problem for Dogs'); RHS's 'Potentially harmful' warning is unscoped by animal and was not used to establish pet scope on its own.

soil_base and soil_drainage rely on MoBot's species-specific Culture prose and NC State's/RHS's structured fields; RHS's Cultivation paragraph ('Under glass grow in peat-free, loam-based potting compost...') was excluded as greenhouse/genus-style boilerplate rather than species-specific guidance.

NC State's page structurally notes that Asparagus setaceus 'is often confused with' Asparagus densiflorus Sprengeri Group, which NC State treats on its own separate page; that species' care was not merged into this record.

records.name_note: NC State renders this species entry both as a combined species page (H1 'Capsicum chinense') whose 'Common Name(s)' list is alphabetized -- Carolina Reaper, Habanero, Habanero Pepper, Habanero Type Pepper -- and as auto-generated per-common-name views, each of which promotes its own name to the H1 and lists the other three under 'Other Common Name(s)'. Because each view titles itself, the choice rests on the names themselves: 'Carolina Reaper' is excluded as a cultivar, which NC State's own Cultivars / Varieties block on this page confirms ('Carolina Reaper', 'Developed in SC; hottest pepper officially recorded as of 2019'), and 'Habanero Pepper' is taken as the fullest species-level common form, matching the H1 of https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/capsicum-chinense/common-name/habanero-pepper/.
unknowns: RHS and MoBot were found and consulted after all, contrary to the research note: RHS carries https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/217770/capsicum-chinense-habanero-group/details (heading 'Capsicum chinense Habanero Group', common name 'chilli pepper Habanero Group') and MoBot carries https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=287204 (heading 'Capsicum chinense'). Neither displaces common_name -- the RHS entry is the Habanero Group rather than the bare species and MoBot's lead common name is the umbrella 'pepper' -- but both were usable for cross-checking, and both confirm Full sun and a moderate moisture regime. RHS's pH field reads 'Acid, Alkaline, or Neutral', which confirms rather than resolves the unbounded pH. No field value changed as a result.

Clemson HGIC's Pepper factsheet is scoped to Capsicum annuum -- a same-genus sibling species already in this catalog as 'Pepper' -- and names habanero only as a cultivar type within it, so none of its day/night temperature ('70 to 85 degrees F during the day and 60 to 70 degrees F during the night'), fertilizing or watering ('to a depth of at least 6 inches') guidance may be borrowed for Capsicum chinense.

Clemson HGIC's Biquinho pepper page is also Capsicum chinense but documents a different common-name pepper type, not Habanero; its care values (e.g. 'top inch of soil to dry between waterings') were not used for Habanero to avoid borrowing a sibling common-name's page content for this species entry.

UF/IFAS Pepper Production (CV130, edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu) gives habanero-cultivar-specific facts (90-100 days to harvest, 100,000-350,000 SHU, ~2x1 in wrinkled fruit) but is a multi-species/multi-cultivar production table rather than a dedicated single-species page, and none of that content maps to a schema field, so it was not used to source or override any field.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: neither NC State page carries a Poison section, and the only value in its structured Problems field is 'Problem for Children', which names neither cats nor dogs, so no citation could satisfy the cats-or-dogs scoping requirement. Hazard text does exist elsewhere and is not cat/dog-scoped either: RHS's entry for this taxon carries 'Irritant if eaten; skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling'.

is_houseplant set to false: NC State's Plant Type field for this species carries Annual, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Vegetable and Warm Season Vegetable with no Houseplant value, its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field reads 10a, 10b, 11a, 11b, and its landscape-use sentence is 'Use these plants in the edible garden.'

chill_damage_f left null: NC State's Capsicum chinense pages state 'Plant only when nighttime temperatures are at least 55F,' which is a transplant-timing guideline, not a stated cold-damage-onset temperature, so it was not used per the rule against deriving chill_damage_f from growing-range/timing figures.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no NC State (species-dedicated) statement of an ideal day or night growing-temperature range was found; the only day/night temperature figures found (Clemson) are genus-level and excluded (see above).

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no admissible species-specific source states a humidity requirement, a footcandle light value, or a species-specific direct-sun-hours figure; NC State's only sun-hours figure is the generic 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' site-wide light-category legend text, excluded per the rule against using that legend for direct_sun_hours_max.

soil_base left null: NC State's Capsicum chinense pages list both a Container landscape location and general garden soil textures (Clay, Loam, Sand, High Organic Matter) with a 12-inch-to-3-foot spacing figure, giving ambiguous support for either garden_bed or a container-based soil_base rather than a clear single enum value.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field renders all three bands -- Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) -- so neither open-ended band yields a bound, and the closed Neutral-band ceiling of 8.0 is not usable either: RHS's entry for this taxon lists pH as 'Acid, Alkaline, or Neutral', which is likewise unbounded, so no independent ceiling exists to confirm one.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est and water_dormant_days_est left null. The moisture statements that do exist were found and rejected on rule grounds, not missed: NC State's culture paragraph opens 'Grow in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun.' and continues 'These plants enjoy heat and tolerate drought, though prolonged drought may affect fruit quality.', and MoBot adds a structured 'Water: Medium' plus 'Easily grown in moist, organically rich, fertile, well-drained soils in full sun.' A soil adjective, a drought-tolerance trait and a mid-scale structured water tag are each expressly barred from setting water_regime, and none of them states a cadence or day interval.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no species-dedicated admissible source (as opposed to Clemson's excluded genus-level Pepper factsheet) gives a fertilizing interval, active season, or dilution strength for Capsicum chinense / Habanero Pepper.
water_estimate_basis left null because no water_regime or day-interval figures were established to base an estimate on.

is_edible is true; the same anchor page also lists, under Problems, "Problem for Children" with no further detail (no named toxic part, severity, toxic principle, or preparation requirement given — just that single tag under the Problems heading).

attracts_pollinators left null: the anchor page's structured "Attracts" field lists only "Songbirds" (explained elsewhere on the page as birds eating the capsaicin-laden fruit unharmed); no bees, butterflies, moths, or hummingbirds are mentioned anywhere on either anchor page, and searches for 'Pollinator', 'butterfl', 'hummingbird' returned 0 hits.

The second anchor URL (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/capsicum-chinense/) rendered as the same NC State page (title: 'Capsicum chinense (Carolina Reaper, Habanero, Habanero Pepper, Habanero Type Pepper)'), not a separate genus-only page with a different range; it contributed no additional size, edibility, or pollinator information beyond the habanero-pepper page.
No pages refused this machine; both anchor URLs returned fetch status ok.

The page separately describes a named cultivar ('Carolina Reaper') as the hottest pepper on record, but the Dimensions block (Height/Width) is presented at the species level, not tied to that cultivar, so it was used as-is; this is not a climbing/vining species, so the size fields were populated normally per rule 4.
